evaluation_cases.prompt_context: When does an int wrap around, and where should I put a double cast if I want a fractional quotient?

items.explanation: A Java int has a fixed 32-bit signed range from Integer.MIN_VALUE to Integer.MAX_VALUE. Adding 1 to Integer.MAX_VALUE wraps to Integer.MIN_VALUE without an exception. Start by predicting the values of Integer.MAX_VALUE - 1, Integer.MAX_VALUE, and Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1, then print each expression and compare it with your prediction. Next trace 7 / 2, (double) 7 / 2, and (double) (7 / 2). The first calculation divides two int operands and yields 3. In the second, one operand is already a double, so the quotient is 3.5. In the third, the int division happens inside the parentheses first and the cast turns the result into 3.0. Write down each operand's type before you run the code. To see that double arithmetic can still round, print 0.1 + 0.2 beside 0.3. Both decimal inputs are approximated in binary. Finish by explaining which operation overflowed, which operation discarded the fractional part, and which operation rounded a floating-point result. Try subtracting 1 from Integer.MIN_VALUE.

resources.title: A Guide to Java Integer Ranges, Signed Overflow, and Explicit Casting: Worked Examples for Tracing Mixed Arithmetic Expressions and Comparing the Results of Integer and Floating-Point Division in Java
AP CS A Primitive Range Textbook Section

resource_evidence.excerpt: The article compares (double) 7 / 2 and (double)(7 / 2), then traces Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1 to Integer.MIN_VALUE using a signed 32-bit number line.
The textbook table lists the signed int extremes and follows a counter through wraparound. A second example compares the binary approximations of 0.1 and 0.2.
The documentation summary introduces Integer.MIN_VALUE and Integer.MAX_VALUE and gives three expressions to check around the endpoints.
